reasons.C1: Real-world detection of self-funded rings on public ledgers matters, but resembles known wash-trading forensics; wallets not shown to be LLM agents.
reasons.C2: Held-out test, permutation and positive control present, yet labels share the rule's evidence, only 10 test families, independent-feature rule p = 0.14.
reasons.C3: 17-page report against an 8-page limit; key result and its circularity caveat risk being buried in length.

levers.C1: Show flagged wallets are actually LLM agents and demonstrate detection against an adaptive ring that knows the four-hop rule.
levers.C2: Obtain labels independent of transfer-graph evidence and test on more families, reporting significance on features labels never used.
levers.C3: Cut to 8 pages with one headline table: held-out accuracy, independent-feature result, and evasion limits up front.

B2.verdict: Grounded in real payment data with honest controls, but the label circularity means we cannot yet tell detection from restatement.

reasons.C1: Testing whether leniency and fines deter LLM cartels is policy-relevant; replaying human lab games with LLMs is an established, growing pattern.
reasons.C2: Nothing runs; plan is preregistered with cut order and fallback, but 48 hours solo for 80 duopolies plus contamination tests is tight.
reasons.C3: Clear problem, plan and single demo table; but no results exist to communicate.

levers.C1: Add an adversarial regime where agents can detect or game the enforcement signal, showing where human-calibrated policy breaks for agents.
levers.C2: Deliver the laissez-faire positive control and all four regimes with intervals and the contamination check actually run.
levers.C3: Present the human-versus-LLM regime table with real intervals and a one-paragraph answer to which rule works on agents.

P3.verdict: Sensible, well-scoped replication plan with a policy angle, but at this point it is a protocol, not a result.

reasons.C1: Unmonitorable vector channels between models are a neglected oversight problem; testing receiver-side countermeasures is a useful, buildable contribution.
reasons.C2: Real models, 10 of 10 checkpoints reproduced, shuffled-label and no-message controls; but channels non-adaptive, trained pre-sprint, no collusion game.
reasons.C3: Figure 1 makes the core finding instantly visible, but 13 pages exceeds the 8-page limit.

levers.C1: Embed the channel in an actual collusion game so the countermeasure is shown to stop coordinated harmful behaviour, not just recall.
levers.C2: Train channels adversarially against snapping and quantization and report whether the defence survives an adaptive attacker with significance tests.
levers.C3: Cut to 8 pages, lead with Figure 1 and state clearly that results hold only for non-adaptive channels.

C2.verdict: Strongest evidence in the field; snapping kills the channel, but any security person asks immediately whether an adaptive channel survives it.

reasons.C1: External actor soliciting price-fixing is a realistic adversarial injection; six-condition design with harmless-request control is thoughtful but conventional.
reasons.C2: 149 tests and frozen preregistration, but no real model run, no model chosen, no results; only mock client runs.
reasons.C3: No report seen, only README dual-use note; design is described but nothing communicates findings.

levers.C1: Vary attacker sophistication and show which framings bypass model refusals, mapping a real attack surface for pricing agents.
levers.C2: Run the 60 preregistered games on two real model families and report acceptance and price shifts with Wilson intervals.
levers.C3: Write the report with a results table per condition, the positive control outcome and the limitations appendix.

C8.verdict: Careful scaffolding and preregistration, but without a single real model run there is nothing yet to judge on outcomes.
